column1: What is a T-SQL stored procedure?
column2:
A named, reusable group of T-SQL statements stored in the database.
A procedure stores a named operation on the database server. A caller supplies its inputs and invokes it with EXEC rather than resending the full implementation.
Review source

column1: How can a stored procedure reduce client-server network traffic?
column2:
The client sends one procedure call instead of its full sequence of statements.
For example, one call can run several related order statements on the server. The client does not need a separate round trip for each step.
Review source

column1: Why centralize shared business rules in a stored procedure?
column2:
Applications can reuse one implementation of the rules.
Applications that call the same procedure use the same rule. A rule change can therefore live in one definition instead of several client implementations.
Review source

column1: Why can a second call to the same SQL Server procedure avoid compiling its statements again?
column2:
Reuse of a cached execution plan.
After compilation, SQL Server can reuse the plan if it remains suitable and cached. The procedure's definition and its cached execution plan are different things.
Review source

column1: A procedure's data distribution changes. Why can its previously cached plan become inefficient?
column2:
Changes to data or table structure can make the original plan a poor fit.
A plan chosen when very few rows matched can perform poorly once the same predicate matches most rows. Recompilation lets the optimizer consider current conditions.
Review source

column1: What client messages does SET NOCOUNT ON suppress during procedure execution?
column2:
Messages reporting the number of rows affected by statements.
NOCOUNT stops per-statement affected-row messages sent to the client. It does not stop SQL Server from keeping @@ROWCOUNT internally.
CREATE PROCEDURE dbo.GetCustomerOrders
    @CustomerID int,
    @StartDate date = NULL
AS
BEGIN
    SET NOCOUNT ON;
    SELECT OrderID
    FROM dbo.Orders
    WHERE CustomerID = @CustomerID
      AND (@StartDate IS NULL OR OrderDate >= @StartDate);
END;
Review source

column1: A procedure uses SET NOCOUNT ON and runs a SELECT. What happens to the SELECT result rows?
column2:
Nothing. The result-set rows are still returned.
A SELECT still sends its rows to the client. NOCOUNT only suppresses separate messages such as the number of rows affected by an UPDATE.
CREATE PROCEDURE dbo.GetCustomerOrders
    @CustomerID int,
    @StartDate date = NULL
AS
BEGIN
    SET NOCOUNT ON;
    SELECT OrderID
    FROM dbo.Orders
    WHERE CustomerID = @CustomerID
      AND (@StartDate IS NULL OR OrderDate >= @StartDate);
END;
Review source

column1: How do input parameters make a stored procedure reusable?
column2:
Callers supply different values without rewriting the procedure.
A parameter such as @CustomerID supplies a different filter value on each call. The procedure's query stays the same.
CREATE PROCEDURE dbo.GetCustomerOrders
    @CustomerID int,
    @StartDate date = NULL
AS
BEGIN
    SET NOCOUNT ON;
    SELECT OrderID
    FROM dbo.Orders
    WHERE CustomerID = @CustomerID
      AND (@StartDate IS NULL OR OrderDate >= @StartDate);
END;
Review source

column1: What must you declare for a scalar procedure parameter to let a caller omit it?
column2:
A declared default value.
If the caller leaves out @StartDate, SQL Server supplies the declared default. The procedure body determines what a NULL date means.
CREATE PROCEDURE dbo.GetCustomerOrders
    @CustomerID int,
    @StartDate date = NULL
AS
BEGIN
    SET NOCOUNT ON;
    SELECT OrderID
    FROM dbo.Orders
    WHERE CustomerID = @CustomerID
      AND (@StartDate IS NULL OR OrderDate >= @StartDate);
END;
Review source

column1: Which parameter kind returns a calculated value to a procedure's caller?
column2:
An OUTPUT parameter.
An OUTPUT parameter carries a value back through a variable. Use it for a value such as a total rather than for a table of order lines.
CREATE PROCEDURE dbo.DoubleValue
    @input int,
    @result int OUTPUT
AS
BEGIN
    SET @result = @input * 2;
END;
GO
DECLARE @value int;
EXEC dbo.DoubleValue @input = 10, @result = @value OUTPUT;
SELECT @value AS Result;
Review source

column1: A caller passes a variable but omits OUTPUT from the EXEC call. What happens to the caller's variable?
column2:
The procedure runs, but the updated value is not copied back.
Without OUTPUT on the call, the caller variable keeps its previous value. The declaration still allows the procedure itself to update the parameter.
CREATE PROCEDURE dbo.DoubleValue
    @input int,
    @result int OUTPUT
AS
BEGIN
    SET @result = @input * 2;
END;
GO
DECLARE @value int;
EXEC dbo.DoubleValue @input = 10, @result = @value OUTPUT;
SELECT @value AS Result;
Review source

column1: How can a stored procedure send tabular query results to its caller?
column2:
Execute a SELECT that returns rows rather than assigning variables.
A SELECT that produces rows sends them to the caller. A SELECT that only assigns a variable does not produce that tabular result.
Review source

column1: What does RETURN usually send in a stored procedure, apart from any SELECT results?
column2:
Exit the procedure and return an integer execution-status code.
RETURN exits immediately with an integer code. Send business values through result sets or output parameters so callers do not confuse data with status.
CREATE PROCEDURE dbo.CheckInput @value int
AS
BEGIN
    IF @value < 0
        RETURN 1;
    RETURN 0;
END;
GO
DECLARE @status int;
EXEC @status = dbo.CheckInput @value = 10;
SELECT @status AS Status;
Review source

column1: How must a stored procedure report failure instead of relying only on RETURN -1?
column2:
Raise an error, for example with THROW.
RETURN -1 only sends a status value that a caller can ignore. THROW raises an exception that the caller or an enclosing CATCH can handle.
Review source

column1: Where does control go after a catchable error occurs in a procedure's TRY block?
column2:
To the associated CATCH block.
Control skips the rest of the TRY block. The CATCH can inspect the error and decide how to clean up or rethrow.
BEGIN TRY
    BEGIN TRANSACTION;
    UPDATE dbo.Orders SET Status = 'Closed' WHERE OrderID = 1;
    COMMIT TRANSACTION;
END TRY
BEGIN CATCH
    IF @@TRANCOUNT > 0
        ROLLBACK TRANSACTION;
    THROW;
END CATCH;
Review source

column1: When must a procedure validate inputs that are required for its data modifications?
column2:
Before it performs those modifications.
Check required values before the first write. For example, reject a missing order ID before changing inventory for that order.
IF @CustomerID IS NULL OR @CustomerID <= 0
    THROW 50001, 'CustomerID must be positive.', 1;
Review source

column1: Why does IF @CustomerID <= 0 fail to reject a missing SQL customer ID?
column2:
NULL <= 0 evaluates to UNKNOWN, not TRUE.
An IF branch runs only when its condition is true, so a comparison alone misses SQL NULL. Add IS NULL to reject that input explicitly.
IF @CustomerID IS NULL OR @CustomerID <= 0
    THROW 50001, 'CustomerID must be positive.', 1;
Review source

column1: Which transaction statements make several procedure writes succeed or roll back together?
column2:
BEGIN TRANSACTION, followed by COMMIT or ROLLBACK.
BEGIN TRANSACTION starts the explicit unit of work. COMMIT keeps its changes, while ROLLBACK reverses them. BEGIN and END only group statements.
BEGIN TRY
    BEGIN TRANSACTION;
    UPDATE dbo.Orders SET Status = 'Closed' WHERE OrderID = 1;
    COMMIT TRANSACTION;
END TRY
BEGIN CATCH
    IF @@TRANCOUNT > 0
        ROLLBACK TRANSACTION;
    THROW;
END CATCH;
Review source

column1: In a procedure that owns its transaction, why check @@TRANCOUNT before ROLLBACK in CATCH?
column2:
To avoid rolling back when no transaction remains active.
Some errors leave no transaction to roll back. A positive count tells you one exists, but use XACT_STATE() if you also need to know whether it can commit.
BEGIN TRY
    BEGIN TRANSACTION;
    UPDATE dbo.Orders SET Status = 'Closed' WHERE OrderID = 1;
    COMMIT TRANSACTION;
END TRY
BEGIN CATCH
    IF @@TRANCOUNT > 0
        ROLLBACK TRANSACTION;
    THROW;
END CATCH;
Review source

column1: A caller already has an open transaction. What risk does a full ROLLBACK in its nested procedure create?
column2:
It also rolls back the caller's transaction.
Nested BEGIN TRANSACTION calls do not create independent transactions. A full rollback unwinds the outer work too, rather than rolling back just the nested procedure.
Review source

column1: Which error-raising statement does Microsoft recommend instead of RAISERROR for new applications?
column2:
THROW.
THROW is the recommendation for new code and honors SET XACT_ABORT. Use a bare THROW inside CATCH to preserve the error that was caught.
BEGIN TRY
    BEGIN TRANSACTION;
    UPDATE dbo.Orders SET Status = 'Closed' WHERE OrderID = 1;
    COMMIT TRANSACTION;
END TRY
BEGIN CATCH
    IF @@TRANCOUNT > 0
        ROLLBACK TRANSACTION;
    THROW;
END CATCH;
Review source

column1: Why rethrow with bare THROW in CATCH instead of raising a new error with the same message?
column2:
To rethrow the original error with its original details.
Bare THROW sends the caught error onward instead of raising a replacement. Building a new error from its text does not preserve details such as the original error number.
BEGIN TRY
    BEGIN TRANSACTION;
    UPDATE dbo.Orders SET Status = 'Closed' WHERE OrderID = 1;
    COMMIT TRANSACTION;
END TRY
BEGIN CATCH
    IF @@TRANCOUNT > 0
        ROLLBACK TRANSACTION;
    THROW;
END CATCH;
Review source

column1: Why schema-qualify procedure and table names?
column2:
To make object resolution explicit and avoid ambiguity.
Using dbo.GetCustomerOrders tells SQL Server which schema to use. That avoids ambiguity when another schema has an object with the same name.
EXEC dbo.GetCustomerOrders @CustomerID = 1001;
Review source

column1: How does an explicit SELECT list protect a procedure's result when a base table gets a new column?
column2:
To keep the returned column contract deliberate and stable.
An explicit SELECT list keeps the names, order, and number of columns intentional. Adding an unrelated base column does not silently add it to the result.
Review source

column1: Why avoid the sp_ prefix for user-defined stored procedures?
column2:
SQL Server uses it for system procedures.
SQL Server uses this prefix for its system procedures. A matching name can cause SQL Server to resolve the system procedure instead.
Review source

column1: Which permission allows a user to run a stored procedure?
column2:
EXECUTE on the procedure.
EXECUTE allows the caller to invoke the procedure. Access inside it can still depend on execution context and ownership, especially for dynamic SQL.
GRANT EXECUTE ON OBJECT::dbo.GetCustomerOrders TO ReportUser;
Review source
